title: Introduction; move to Idaho
description: Dale Anderson introduces the interview with Elizabeth Mabbutt, recorded in St. Mary's, Idaho. Mabbutt describes her 1930 move from Michigan to Idaho with four others in a Chevrolet Sport Coupe.

title: Family background
description: Mabbutt provides details about her parents, including their names, birthdates, and occupations. She also discusses her siblings, their careers, and her husband's background.

title: Courtship and marriage
description: Mabbutt recounts meeting her husband, their courtship, marriage in Spokane, and his work as a cook. She also mentions his prior children and their ranch upbringing.

title: Employment and travel
description: Mabbutt outlines her work history as a bank teller, waitress, and employment office manager. She also discusses her love of travel, trips with her sister, and impressions of Alaska.

title: Homesteading experiences
description: Mabbutt describes her homesteading experiences at Dividual Creek, including building a cabin and living in isolation. She reflects on the challenges and rewards of homestead life.

title: Community involvement; rural life
description: Mabbutt discusses her involvement in groups like the PEO Sisterhood and reflects on the advantages and disadvantages of rural living, including isolation and community connections.

title: Recreation and family life
description: Mabbutt talks about childhood recreation, including movies and card games, and contrasts it with her married life during the Depression. She also discusses her husband's work and their move to town.

title: Marriage reflections; widowhood
description: Mabbutt reflects on her expectations for marriage, her stepchildren, and the adjustments she faced after becoming a widow, including solitude and decision-making.

title: Depression era; gardening
description: Mabbutt discusses the impact of the Depression on her life and work opportunities. She also describes her gardening experiences, particularly with raspberries.

title: Media and leisure activities
description: Mabbutt lists the newspapers and magazines she reads and discusses her leisure activities, including movie outings and travel with friends.

title: Closing remarks
description: Mabbutt concludes the interview by mentioning Harvey Creek and Dividual Creek, tying back to her homesteading experiences. Anderson wraps up the session.

title: Divigio name; CCC camps; roads, mail and trains
description: Elizabeth Mabbutt explains the naming of Divigio and describes the isolated river community before roads. She recounts how CCC camps built the road during the Depression, how lumberjacks carried mail up from Calder, and how passenger trains and flag stops were the main transportation to Spokane.

title: Schooling; snowshoe trail to the homestead
description: She tells of three young girls from Marble Creek who rode horseback to school at Herrick and wintered in a rented cabin nearby. She then describes the steep two- to three-mile trail, crossed by suspension bridges, that required snowshoes to reach the family homestead.

title: Bears at the cabin; hunting and bear meat
description: Mabbutt recounts frightening night visits by bears, including one breaking a window and later tearing through the roof to reach stored huckleberries and sugar. She also recalls her father shooting a young bear at Harvey Creek and her inability to eat bear meat because the skinned carcass looked too human.

title: Abandoned logging camps; salvaging supplies
description: She describes deserted Weyerhaeuser logging camps left during the Depression, whose abandoned supplies homesteaders freely scavenged. Her family took enamel dishes and windows after bears broke theirs.

title: Mail-order groceries; bulk buying and bread baking
description: Mabbutt explains ordering groceries once or twice a year from Burgundy's catalog in Spokane, buying hundred-pound sacks of sugar and flour, and the excitement of unpacking the order. She and Dale Anderson discuss baking their own bread.

title: Arrival of electricity; conveniences in St. Mary's
description: She contrasts her electrified Michigan childhood with homestead life, recalling battery radios that failed just before Pearl Harbor and Roosevelt's death. She discusses the value of refrigerators, electric stoves, and the hardship of open-kettle canning on a wood stove.

title: Reflections on homestead life; love of the outdoors
description: Mabbutt comments on young people returning to the land and reflects that her hard homestead years were among the most wonderful of her life. She attributes her happiness to the beautiful, roadless country and her lifelong love of walking.
